result.markdown: --- title: "Session 4 — Comparing Two Groups on a Number" subtitle: "One-sample t · Welch t · paired t · Mann–Whitney · Wilcoxon signed-rank · effect sizes · what each result means · Lab 4" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - Session 2: checking shape and spread; Session 3: category outcomes - Today: the outcome is a **number**, compared with a benchmark, between **two groups**, or **before and after** - By the end you can: - run the t-test that fits the design, and its **rank-based partner** - say what each test **actually compares** (means, a location shift, a pseudo-median) - report a **difference with its 95% CI** and an **effect size** - tell a **precise** non-significant result from an **imprecise** one ::: # Topic 1 — One group against a benchmark {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## One-sample t: fasting glucose against 100 mg/dL ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} t.test(p$fbs_presentation, mu = 100) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` One Sample t-test data: p$fbs_presentation t = 16.437, df = 630, p-value < 2.2e-16 alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 100 95 percent confidence interval: 107.9482 110.1049 sample estimates: mean of x 109.0266 ``` ::: ::: ## z or t? ::: {.incremental} - A **z-test** needs the **population** SD to be **known** in advance; in practice it almost never is - The SD we compute from our sample is an **estimate** → use the **t-test**, whatever the sample size - "z if n > 30" is an old shortcut from printed tables: with large n the t and z answers agree anyway, so nothing is gained by switching ::: ::: {.key} Default: `t.test()`. A z-test only if a published population SD is used, and say so. ::: ## Reading the one-sample result ::: {.eq} "Mean fasting glucose at presentation was 109.0 mg/dL (95% CI 107.9 to 110.1), 9.0 mg/dL above the 100 mg/dL threshold for impaired fasting glucose (one-sample t-test, p < 0.001)." ::: - The benchmark must come from **outside** the data (a clinical cut-off, a national survey), chosen **before** the analysis - The CI is narrow because n is large: the **average** adult here is above the threshold, though many individuals are not # Topic 2 — Two independent groups {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Welch t: age by diabetes history ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p |> group_by(past_history_of_diabetes) |> summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(age_of_participants), sd = sd(age_of_participants)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 4 past_history_of_diabetes n mean sd 1 no 604 42.9 11.4 2 yes 27 53.8 11.1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} t.test(age_of_participants ~ past_history_of_diabetes, data = p) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Welch Two Sample t-test data: age_of_participants by past_history_of_diabetes t = -4.9647, df = 28.475, p-value = 2.928e-05 alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group no and group yes is not equal to 0 95 percent confidence interval: -15.35778 -6.39106 sample estimates: mean in group no mean in group yes 42.94040 53.81481 ``` ::: ::: ## Reading it ::: {.eq} "Adults with a past history of diabetes were older: mean 53.8 vs 42.9 years (difference 10.9 years, 95% CI 6.4 to 15.4; Welch t-test, p < 0.001; Cohen's d = 0.97)." ::: ::: {.incremental} - **Welch**: the groups are very unequal in size (27 vs 604), exactly where Student's t can mislead - The sign: R reports **no − yes**; turn it round so the sentence reads naturally, and say which way - d ≈ 1.0: a **large** difference; diabetes becomes more common with age ::: ## Two non-significant results, two different stories ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Fasting glucose, women vs men** (n = 631) 108.9 vs 109.1 mg/dL, difference 95% CI -2.4 to 2.0; p = 0.848 → **precise**: any difference is under about 2 mg/dL ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Same, in the 27 adults with diabetes** 142.8 vs 150.7 mg/dL, difference 95% CI -17.5 to 1.8; p = 0.105 → **imprecise**: women could be up to 18 mg/dL lower, or slightly higher ::: ::: ::: {.warn} Both are "not significant". Only the **confidence interval** tells you whether the study **showed** little difference or simply **could not tell**. ::: ## Mann–Whitney U: glucose by diabetes history ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p |> group_by(past_history_of_diabetes) |> summarise(n = n(), median = median(glucose_level_mg_d_l), q1 = quantile(glucose_level_mg_d_l, .25), q3 = quantile(glucose_level_mg_d_l, .75)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 5 past_history_of_diabetes n median q1 q3 1 no 604 106 96 115 2 yes 27 200 158 240 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} wilcox.test(glucose_level_mg_d_l ~ past_history_of_diabetes, data = p, conf.int = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction data: glucose_level_mg_d_l by past_history_of_diabetes W = 1224.5, p-value = 7.528e-14 alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0 95 percent confidence interval: -115.00008 -71.00002 sample estimates: difference in location -93.99999 ``` ::: ::: ## What Mann–Whitney actually tests ::: {.incremental} - It ranks all values and asks whether one group tends to have **higher values** than the other - It is **not** a test of medians unless the two distributions have the **same shape** - `conf.int = TRUE` gives the **Hodges–Lehmann** shift: the typical difference between a person in one group and a person in the other - Effect size **r** = Z / √N: 0.30 here (rough guide: 0.1 small, 0.3 medium, 0.5 large) ::: ::: {.eq} "Glucose was higher in adults with a history of diabetes: median 200 (IQR 158–240) vs 106 (96–115) mg/dL; Mann–Whitney U test, p < 0.001; Hodges–Lehmann shift 94 mg/dL (95% CI 71 to 115)." ::: # Topic 3 — Paired measurements {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Paired t: fasting glucose at presentation and 6 months ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} d <- p$fbs_presentation - p$fbs_6_months c(mean = mean(d), sd = sd(d), skewness = skew(d)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mean sd skewness 10.40266244 6.60438831 -0.04241131 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} t.test(p$fbs_presentation, p$fbs_6_months, paired = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Paired t-test data: p$fbs_presentation and p$fbs_6_months t = 39.566, df = 630, p-value < 2.2e-16 alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0 95 percent confidence interval: 9.886364 10.918961 sample estimates: mean difference 10.40266 ``` ::: ::: ## Reading the paired result ::: {.eq} "Fasting glucose fell by a mean of 10.4 mg/dL from presentation to 6 months (95% CI 9.9 to 10.9; paired t-test, p < 0.001; d~z~ = 1.58)." ::: ::: {.incremental} - The assumption is about the **differences** (skewness -0.04: fine), not about either column - The effect size for paired data is **d~z~** = mean difference / SD of the differences - **Why paired?** Each person is their own control. The visits are strongly correlated (r = 0.91): a person high at presentation stays high - Ignoring the pairing (Welch) gives a 95% CI of 8.8 to 12.0, about 3 times **wider**: the between-person spread swamps the change ::: ## Wilcoxon signed-rank: systolic pressure, presentation and 6 months ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wilcox.test(p$sbp_presentation, p$sbp_6_months, paired = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Wilcoxon signed rank test with continuity correction data: p$sbp_presentation and p$sbp_6_months V = 172556, p-value < 2.2e-16 alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0 95 percent confidence interval: 7.000042 8.500018 sample estimates: (pseudo)median 7.999917 ``` ::: ::: - For paired data that are **skewed or have outliers** (SBP at presentation: skewness 0.48, up to 209 mmHg) - Assumes the differences are **roughly symmetric** (skewness 0.12); it estimates the **pseudo-median** fall: 8 mmHg (95% CI 7 to 9) - Here the paired t-test would also be fine; with real outliers or a small sample, Wilcoxon is the safer choice ## Which test for two groups? | Design | Roughly normal | Skewed / outliers / ordinal | Report | |---|---|---|---| | One group vs benchmark | one-sample t | one-sample Wilcoxon | mean (95% CI) | | Two independent groups | **Welch t** | **Mann–Whitney U** | difference in means (95% CI), d; or medians (IQR), HL shift, r | | Two paired measurements | **paired t** (differences normal) | **Wilcoxon signed-rank** | mean difference (95% CI), d~z~; or pseudo-median | ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 4 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `stats-workshop/labs/lab4_two_groups.R` - a one-sample t-test against a clinical benchmark - Welch t-test with Cohen's d, and the sentence - Mann–Whitney with the Hodges–Lehmann shift and r - paired t-test: check the differences, then test - Wilcoxon signed-rank for skewed paired data ::: **Time:** 35 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t4q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="nggcbf.fsx9wr" data-show="QSBvbmUtc2FtcGxlIHQtdGVzdCwgYmVjYXVzZSB0aGUgU0QgaXMgZXN0aW1hdGVk" data-explain="VGhlIHotdGVzdCBuZWVkcyBhIGtub3duIHBvcHVsYXRpb24gU0QuIEFuIFNEIGVzdGltYXRl ZCBmcm9tIHRoZSBzYW1wbGUgY2FsbHMgZm9yIHRoZSB0LXRlc3Q7IHdpdGggbGFyZ2UgbiB0 aGUgdHdvIGdpdmUgbmVhcmx5IHRoZSBzYW1lIGFuc3dlciwgc28gdGhlcmUgaXMgbm8gcmVh c29uIHRvIHN3aXRjaC4="} You compare a sample mean with a reference value and estimate the SD from your own 200 participants. Which test? - A one-sample z-test, because n is more than 30 - A one-sample t-test, because the SD is estimated - A paired t-test, because there are two values involved - A Mann-Whitney test, because there is only one group ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t4q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="nggpk5.fsxoe5" data-show="QSBzaG93cyBhbnkgZGlmZmVyZW5jZSBpcyBzbWFsbDsgQiBjYW5ub3QgcnVsZSBvdXQgYSBs YXJnZSBvbmU=" data-explain="Tm9uLXNpZ25pZmljYW50IHJlc3VsdHMgZGlmZmVyIGluIHByZWNpc2lvbi4gQSdzIG5hcnJv dyBpbnRlcnZhbCBydWxlcyBvdXQgYSBtZWFuaW5nZnVsIGRpZmZlcmVuY2U7IEIncyB3aWRl IGludGVydmFsIGlzIGNvbXBhdGlibGUgd2l0aCBubyBkaWZmZXJlbmNlIGFuZCB3aXRoIGEg bGFyZ2Ugb25lLg=="} Study A: p = 0.61, 95% CI for the difference -0.6 to 1.0. Study B: p = 0.13, 95% CI -1.6 to 12.2. Which reading is right? - Both studies have shown that there is no difference at all - Study B is the stronger evidence because its p is smaller - A shows any difference is small; B cannot rule out a large one - Neither study can be interpreted, since both p-values exceed 0.05 ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t4q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="ngh2st.fsy2vh" data-show="T25lIGdyb3VwIHRlbmRzIHRvIGhhdmUgaGlnaGVyIGdsdWNvc2UgdmFsdWVzIHRoYW4gdGhl IG90aGVy" data-explain="TWFubi1XaGl0bmV5IGNvbXBhcmVzIHRoZSByYW5rczogd2hldGhlciB2YWx1ZXMgaW4gb25l IGdyb3VwIHRlbmQgdG8gZXhjZWVkIHRob3NlIGluIHRoZSBvdGhlci4gSXQgaXMgYSB0ZXN0 IG9mIG1lZGlhbnMgb25seSB3aGVuIHRoZSB0d28gZGlzdHJpYnV0aW9ucyBoYXZlIHRoZSBz YW1lIHNoYXBlLg=="} Glucose is strongly skewed in both groups and the shapes differ. What does a significant Mann-Whitney test allow you to say? - The two groups have different median glucose values - One group tends to have higher glucose values than the other - The mean glucose values of the two groups differ significantly - The variances of glucose in the two groups are not the same ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t4q4" data-type="fill" data-hashes="oxhcvw.ro183z,mf62mp.z75td5,i08uhv.v0ewz3" data-show="ZGlmZmVyZW5jZXM=" data-explain="ZHogPSBtZWFuIGRpZmZlcmVuY2UgLyBTRCBvZiB0aGUgZGlmZmVyZW5jZXMuIFVzaW5nIHRo ZSBTRCBvZiBlaXRoZXIgdmlzaXQgaW5zdGVhZCBnaXZlcyBhIGRpZmZlcmVudCBudW1iZXIg YW5kIG11c3QgYmUgbGFiZWxsZWQgYXMgc3VjaC4="} For a paired t-test, the effect size dz is the mean of the differences divided by the standard deviation of the ____ . (one word) ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t4q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="nghta8.fsyvu8" data-show="V2lsY294b24gc2lnbmVkLXJhbmsgdGVzdCBvbiB0aGUgcGFpcmVkIG1lYXN1cmVtZW50cw==" data-explain="U2FtZSBwZW9wbGUgdHdpY2UgbWVhbnMgcGFpcmVkIGRhdGE7IHdpdGggc2tld2VkIGRpZmZl cmVuY2VzLCB0aGUgV2lsY294b24gc2lnbmVkLXJhbmsgdGVzdC4gTWFubi1XaGl0bmV5IGFu ZCBXZWxjaCB0cmVhdCB0aGUgdmlzaXRzIGFzIGluZGVwZW5kZW50IGdyb3VwcywgYW5kIGN1 dHRpbmcgYSBudW1iZXIgaW50byBjYXRlZ29yaWVzIHRocm93cyBpbmZvcm1hdGlvbiBhd2F5 Lg=="} The same adults had systolic pressure measured at presentation and at 6 months; the differences are skewed. Which test fits? - Mann-Whitney U test on the two sets of measurements - Welch t-test, because the two visits have unequal spread - Wilcoxon signed-rank test on the paired measurements - Chi-square test after splitting each reading at 140 ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - **t, not z**, whenever the SD comes from your sample - Two groups: **Welch t** or **Mann–Whitney**; paired: **paired t** (differences normal) or **Wilcoxon signed-rank** - Every result: the **difference with its 95% CI**, an **effect size**, then p - A non-significant p with a **wide** CI means "we cannot tell", not "no difference" ::: **Next:** Session 5: more than two groups, repeated measures, correlation and reporting

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
